newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE - Technology and Torah fused at Israel institute.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Technology and Torah fused at Israel institute.

text.p: What do you do if you're an Orthodox Jewish space scientist and urgently need to send a signal to your malfunctioning satellite on the Jewish Sabbath, when religious law forbids you to use electricity?
The solution might be found in a cluttered stone cottage in Jerusalem, the unlikely nexus between modern technology and the 3,000-year-old compendium of Jewish law known as Halacha.

The engineers and rabbis of the Institute of Science and Halacha will consult their toolkits and the Torah to devise a Sabbath computer keyboard so you can tune up your orbiting spacecraft with a rabbinical seal of approval.
"We don't modify Jewish law to meet changing technology. We modify technology to meet Jewish law," said David Bannett, an electrical engineer and consultant to the institute.
Rabbi Levi Yitzhak Halperin, an ultra-Orthodox Jew whose bright, deep-set eyes are framed by a black skullcap and a flowing white beard, is the institute's Halacha chief and theological guide.

Seated in a cramped office with peeling paint and polyester curtains, Halperin probes leather-bound Hebrew and Aramaic tomes to elucidate ancient parallels to modern dilemmas ranging from human cloning to carrying corpses on airplanes -- a problem of ritual purity for members of Judaism's priestly caste.
"We are now working on electric wheelchairs for the Sabbath," said Halperin. "Also on wheelchairs that work on air pressure."
The institute consecrates a great deal of energy to the use of electricity on the Sabbath, the divinely ordained day of rest stretching from sundown on Friday to sundown on Saturday.

On the Sabbath, the Torah forbids Jews from engaging in 39 specific biblical categories of "work", including lighting a fire -- extended in today's world to a prohibition on flicking on and off light switches or starting a car.
THE "INDIRECT-ACTION SWITCH"

The electricity ban doesn't mean Orthodox Jews sit around in the dark all Sabbath. Lights left on before Friday sundown may remain on. A non-Jew can flip the switch. Or a timer can be set before the Sabbath to turn off the lights at a specific hour.
But the institute has patented a smarter gadget which opens up new horizons for Sabbath electricity -- the "indirect-action switch".
It works by extension of a simple principle: the Halacha permits one to block out a light on the Sabbath by covering it with a shutter.
The switch is essentially a light-sensitive electrical circuit that is left on before the Sabbath and is continually interrupted by a tiny light that pulsates about every tenth of a second.
As long as the light continues to hit the circuit, any appliance connected to it will remain off.
If a religious Jew wants to turn on the appliance, he flicks a switch that draws a shutter over the pulsing light. The circuit is then complete and power flows to the appliance.
"Separating the person from the final action makes him not legally responsible," Bannett said. "You can avoid the problem by getting around it."
The institute's engineers have wired the switches into emergency telephones, hospital call buttons and cardkeys for electric hotel doors.
"We can put it into computer keyboards so you can have a Sabbath-observant Jewish satellite," chuckled Bannett.
The institute's rebuttal to the switch's critics -- who say it amounts to pulling the wool over God's eyes -- is as dexterous as the device itself.
"There are loopholes in the law. Is this fooling God? No. The loopholes are God-given loopholes," Bannett said.
